sources.title: Go with the flow - not a motto for fish!
Máy Lọc Bể Cá: Cách Chọn Đúng Theo Kích Thước Hồ Và Loại Cá Nuôi - Thủy Sinh 24
Bể Cá Betta Có Lọc: Hướng Dẫn Chi Tiết Từ A Đến Z
Aquarium Basics: Water Flow & Circulation – Green Chapter
Sewellia lineolata (Tiger Hillstream Loach) · Seriously Fish
How to Improve Water Circulation on Aquarium Sponge Filters

facts.fact: Vietnamese term for water flow/current: "dòng chảy".
Vietnamese term for flow rate: "Lưu lượng", given in "L/h" or as "lần/giờ" (times per hour).
Vietnamese term used for a filter's water flow rate: "Lưu Lượng Nước (GPH/LPH)".
Vietnamese term for a filter's outflow current: "dòng trả nước".
Vietnamese term for a flow reducer fitted to a filter outlet: "bộ giảm dòng".
Vietnamese term for a dead spot (an area where water does not circulate and waste can build up): "điểm chết".
Water flow carries oxygen-rich water through the tank, moves waste toward the filter, spreads heater warmth evenly and circulates nutrients and CO₂ in planted tanks.
Circulation mixes water from top to bottom so oxygen and temperature stay even, and helps carbon dioxide and excess nitrogen escape to the air.
Surface movement lets carbon dioxide escape and fresh oxygen dissolve into the water.
Good current spreads oxygen, fertilizer and food and keeps debris from collecting in stagnant spots.
Some fish do not spawn without water movement: one barbel keeper's barbels and danionins that had never bred spawned within two weeks of adding flow pumps.
In the wild, barbels and danionins seek fast water in clear streams to catch passing plankton.
Freshwater currents range from none in lakes, to gentle in lowlands and larger rivers, to strong in mountain areas; the author measured river and stream currents of 1.4 to 11 km/h.
The aim is balanced water movement across the tank, not the strongest possible flow.
Aeration should keep dissolved oxygen above 5.0 mg/L throughout the system.
Too-strong flow: fish swim constantly against the current, tails get swept, or fish shelter in one corner of the tank.
Too-strong flow can push fish against the walls, tear tails, and cause stress and refusal to eat.
Betta fish that keep looking for hiding places, swim with difficulty or are pushed adrift are in too strong a current; too much flow stresses, exhausts and can injure them.
Too little flow: waste collects in corners and low-flow areas, and a surface film forms in calm areas.
Signs of low oxygen from poor circulation may show near morning hours.
An outflow that is weaker than usual means the filter media are clogged.
Dead spots form behind rocks or wood and in dirty substrate pockets; dense hardscape often creates hidden dead zones.
Actual flow falls 20-30% as filter media get dirty, and clogged filter wool can cut actual flow by 50-70% without the keeper noticing.
Intake sponges that are never cleaned make flow weaken gradually.
Flow drops quickly with distance: an 800 l/h internal filter gave 1.4 km/h at 10 cm and 1.3 km/h at 30 cm; a 2,000 l/h submersible pump gave 2.16 km/h at 10 and 30 cm but no measurable flow at 80 cm.
A wide jet pipe reduced the filter's flow somewhat and a spray bar reduced it to zero in JBL's tests.
Formula given: filter flow (L/h) = tank volume (L) × a multiplier for the fish kept, minimum 5–12 times per hour depending on species.
Planted tanks with small fish (neon, tetra, shrimp): 5-8 times per hour, e.g. a 100 L tank needs a 500-800 L/h filter, with weak flow so plants are not disturbed.

Ordinary community tanks (goldfish, molly, gourami): 5-10 times per hour; large or fast-swimming fish (discus, arowana, cichlids): 8-12 times per hour; outdoor koi ponds: 3-5 times per hour with very large biological media.
Choose a filter whose rated output on the box is 20–30% above the calculated need, because real flow is lower.
For a betta tank, flow of about 2-4 times the tank volume per hour is suggested, e.g. a filter of about 20-40 LPH for a 10 litre tank.
To reduce flow for bettas: set the filter to its lowest setting, put a sponge on the hang-on filter outlet, and aim the outflow at the tank wall rather than into the swimming space.
Choose a filter with an adjustable flow knob, or add homemade sponge baffles.
Adjust the filter output direction gradually and watch where debris settles to check that every area gets some movement.
Recheck flow after changing hardscape or equipment; reposition hardscape if large stagnant zones form; add circulation pumps only if needed.
With the Aquarium Co-Op Easy Flow spout, aim it at the front wall to push mulm toward the middle and back where the filter can pick it up; raise it to the waterline for more surface agitation.
If surface current from a sponge filter is too strong for top-dwelling fish, reduce it with the air pump's flow control or an air valve.
JBL says flow pumps, unlike filters, are the only real way to create a targeted current, and flow should be measured where the fish will live, not only at the outlet.
Aim for a gentle surface ripple without heavy splashing; perfectly still surface water reduces oxygen exchange.
Do not aim strong flow straight at plants, but make sure circulation reaches lower plant areas; CO₂ systems depend on stable circulation.
Clean clogged sponges and intake guards before flow drops significantly.
Weak flow is the top priority for small, weak-swimming fish; strong flow stresses and exhausts them.
Betta need very light flow; avoid canister or submersible filters with strong flow for them, and shield or adjust submersible filter outflow.
Sponge filters are gentle enough that they will not suck up fry, dwarf shrimp or long-finned betta, though their flow is sometimes too weak to circulate the tank well.
Discus should avoid strong direct flow, arowana need steady flow that causes no stress, while koi tolerate stronger circulation.
Vigorous aeration of submerged filter beds can dislodge beneficial bacteria.
Using too strong a filter in a small tank for betta or small fish.
A filter designed for a 50 litre tank is too strong for a 5-10 litre betta tank.
Forgetting that actual flow drops as media get dirty, and not replacing mechanical filter wool regularly.
Assuming stronger flow is always better; excess current stresses fish, uproots plants and creates unstable flow patterns.
Blocking flow with hardscape and ignoring dead spots and debris patterns.
Assuming a filter outlet makes a strong current or that a pump's rated output equals usable flow where the fish are.
Installing an internal filter facing the wrong way can make too much turbulence for Betta.
Thủy Sinh 24 warns that if the pump stops in a power cut for a few hours, anaerobic bacteria produce toxins; oxygen falls and the filter's bacteria suffer, so fish can become stressed very quickly.
Large tanks often run into trouble in power cuts lasting many hours, especially in hot weather; switching a filter off is especially dangerous when it is hot or the tank is heavily stocked.
After a power cut, change part of the water with dechlorinated water if toxin readings rise, instead of just switching the filter back on.
Sewellia lineolata, a hillstream loach native to Vietnam, needs a strong current and well-oxygenated water; Seriously Fish suggests a filter that ideally turns the tank over 15-20 times per hour.
Sewellia lineolata is kept at 20–24°C and tolerates warmer water only if its oxygen needs are met.
Flow-loving fish either hold position in the current using little energy or cling to the substrate with suction organs or fins modified into adhesive organs, as gobies do.
Finer bubbles move oxygen more efficiently; cutting bubble size from 5 mm to 2 mm can improve mixing and transfer almost fivefold.
Porous air diffusers clog with algae, food and waste and need periodic cleaning; in water with alkalinity over 400 mg/L as CaCO₃, carbonate can block stone diffusers.
